newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: IRA aims to wear down UK public.
newsitem.headline: IRA aims to wear down UK public.

text.p: IRA guerrillas are hoping that the British public's weariness with travel chaos will push the country's political leaders into concessions in Northern Ireland, security sources in Ireland say.
London's Monday morning traffic chaos is apparently the latest example of tactics which aim at maximum disruption, maximum publicity and minimum loss of life, the sources said.

In the run-up to Britain's May 1 elections, Irish Republican Army guerrillas fighting to end British rule of Northern Ireland have shifted the focus of their 28-year war to the mainland in the hope that the next British government will ease conditions for its entry to peace talks.
The long-held belief in the shadowy Irish Republican leadership is that the people of Britain are weary of the Northern Ireland conflict which has killed 3,200 people.
The 1.5 million people of the British province of Northern Ireland have spent most of the past quarter-century living under the protection of almost 20,000 British troops and 13,000 armed police.
Army checkpoints, helicopter surveillance flights and the sight of fully-armed soldiers strolling the streets of every Northern Ireland town are part of the province's way of life.

By bringing the conflict to the streets of London, IRA commanders hope that British public opinion will push the next British government towards fashioning a solution that meets their Irish nationalist agenda.
They are encouraged by opinion polls carried out in the early 1990s which suggest that most British people would like to "get rid of" the Northern Ireland problem.
An IRA bombing campaign in major British cities began as long ago as the 1950s.

But the guerrillas are apparently keeping their stocks of deadly Semtex plastic explosive under wraps at present for fear of causing a wave of popular revulsion that would deepen its international isolation, the sources said.

It may be no coincidence that, at the same time, there has been a sharp drop in attacks in Northern Ireland itself by the IRA while its political wing, Sinn Fein, campaigns for votes in the May 1 poll, the sources said.

Sinn Fein wants the next British administration to use economic force and political argument to make the leaders of Northern Ireland's pro-British Unionist politicians sit down and negotiate with their sworn foes, Sinn Fein.

But the Unionists, whose war cry is "No Surrender" say they will never negotiate with a political party which has a private army ready to contest with bombs and bullets any settlement that does not satisfy it.

Nor is there any sign that Britain's opposition Labour party, which is widely expected to form the next British government, will ease the ban imposed by British Prime Minister John Major on Sinn Fein's entry into the peace talks until the IRA ends its war for good.
Monday's bomb warnings, for which no group has yet claimed responsibility, were issued 24 hours after the Sinn Fein rallied its membership to maximise votes in the election.

Martin McGuinness, de facto deputy leader of Sinn Fein, told the conference that the poll could be a "watershed" for the party and lead to an end to the ban on Sinn Fein taking part in the Belfast negotiations.
He said that a good showing in the poll would "reverberate in the corridors of power in Britain, Dublin and Washington" which have all banned contact with Sinn Fein until the IRA halts its war.

Sinn Fein's conditions for seeking a renewal of a 17-month truce the IRA broke in February 1996 are immediate entry to the peace talks without preconditions and the dropping of any insistence that the IRA start to disarm.

Both Labour and the Conservatives say there can be no deal until the IRA calls a permanent end to its war. Sinn Fein says that is un unacceptable precondition. Security sources do not underestimate the ability of the IRA to create more than havoc; they believe the guerrillas have enough arms, ammunition and explosives to keep fighting well into the 21st century.
Despite a wave of arrests and arms seizures, they fear that the guerrillas remain one of the deadliest, best-armed and organised underground armies in Europe.
